questions.q: A least-squares line with an intercept is fitted to $n$ points. What is $\sum_i e_i$, the sum of the residuals $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$?
options: Exactly 0, because the residual vector is orthogonal to the column of 1s
It is positive whenever there are outliers
questions.explain: The normal equation for $b_0$ says $\sum_i e_i = e \cdot \mathbf 1 = 0$. That is why we square residuals for the loss: their plain sum is always 0 and says nothing about fit quality.

questions.q: The residuals-vs-fitted plot shows a clear U shape (positive at both ends, negative in the middle). What does this suggest?
options: The true relationship is curved, so a straight line is the wrong model
There is a single high-leverage outlier
questions.explain: A systematic pattern in the residuals means the model missed structure — here curvature, so add an $x^2$ feature or use a non-linear model. A growing spread (funnel) would instead indicate heteroscedasticity.

questions.q: A point lies far to the right of all the others in $x$ but its residual is small. Which statement is correct?
options: It has low leverage, because its residual is small
It has high leverage; it may still be influential, because it pulls the line towards itself and so shrinks its own residual
Leverage depends only on $y$, so we cannot tell
Its Cook's distance is always exactly 0
questions.explain: Leverage $h_{ii} = 1/n + (x_i-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}$ depends only on $x$. A high-leverage point drags the line towards itself, so a small residual does not prove it is harmless; Cook's distance (leverage combined with residual) or refitting without the point tells you.

questions.q: For a fitted line, SST = 50 and SSE = 10. What is $R^2$, and what is SSR?
questions.explain: $R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST} = 1 - 10/50 = 0.8$, and SST = SSR + SSE gives SSR = 40. A common trap is computing SSE/SST = 0.2, which is the *unexplained* share.
